utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was a scheduling issue to be raised, I think by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We have -- I have discussed with -- with the Defence with Mr. Cayley, who I see who is not here, and with Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Kehoe, and the possibility of having an extra session next week in light of other plans that are already scheduled, and in light of the schedule, obviously we understand that it's no one's fault, but the schedule's slipping and that the next witness, with the last witness, we wanted to see if there was a way that we could complete his testimony by Wednesday afternoon, and the parties had agreed to have an extra session next week. Just for the sake of transparency, I also had a conversation with the Chamber's legal officer on that issue, and he informed me that there might be a problem with the proposed date of next week, and that's why I wanted to raise the issue with Chamber and see if there was a way, either this week or next week, with the parties' agreement, of course, if we could have at least one extra sitting to ensure that we can have the last -- the next witness complete his testimony by next Wednesday. As he is the last witness, it is also not possible to push him further, so that was the issue that we wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. I think the swap on the 11th from afternoon to morning has been agreed upon and does not meet any objection by the Chamber. Monday, the 9th, and Tuesday, the 10th, to sit the whole day certainly causes some problems. If I just speak for myself at this moment, Tuesday, the 10th, the Rules Committee meets and I'm a bit hesitant to ask all the member of the Rules Committee to find a new date. So on from 11.00 in the morning there would be no problem, but then it is a matter to arrange additional time. On Monday, in the afternoon, my agenda is not empty, let me tell you this. To what extent this can be changed is still to be seen. I suggest that we give the information, as far as other commitments of members of the Chamber, so that we can work to see where time could be gained, together with the Registrar, and the Chamber is certainly not unwilling to cooperate. At the same time, looking at the assessment of time needed, even if we would gain some time, it still might be a rather tight schedule anyhow. So, therefore, the Chamber is willing to accommodate, to the -- to the extent possible. At the same time, it's to some extent also in the hands of the parties to conduct the examination-in-chief and cross-examination in such a way that we could finish by Wednesday, the 11th. Have you considered one afternoon session on the 11th or ... in the afternoon? One small session --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We could have one session in the afternoon, Your Honour, until maybe 4.00 in the afternoon it would be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If would you include that in exploring all the possibilities, then let's see whether we can achieve the result you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We're very grateful to the Chamber and to the parties for their cooperation on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, Mr. Mikulicic, I do understand that even if we would finish on the 11th, that the commencement of the presentation of the Markac Defence would start on the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, on Monday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All the preparation has been done in -- according to that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear further and we'll inform all interested parties, provide them with the information they need to make a new schedule. Then, Ms. Higgins, is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Christopher Albiston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration before you give testimony in this courtroom. And, Mr. Albiston, the text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, you will first be examined by Ms. Higgins. Ms. Higgins is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could you please, first of all, state your full name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Charles Kennedy Albiston.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to start by calling up your report --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The public version, please, which is 2D00768.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, while that is coming up, I hope the operations of the screens have been explained to you, and if there's any problem please just indicate and we'll try and deal with it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you could have a look on the screen, and you see there the first page of a report that you submitted in August 2009, which was filed with the Chamber on the 10th of September, 2009. Is it right that during the course of last week, you prepared a short one-page corrigendum to your report, to deal with some errors which you identified to this report which is before us on the screen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like then to call up the corrigendum, please, so that we have it before us, which is 2D00788.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, while that document is coming up onto the screen, just to put it into context, this is a one-page corrigenda, and it refers to corrections that you have made in the text which we've just seen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, you are addressing Ms. Higgins for the second time as sir. I make similar mistakes now and then, but she --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour. In the jurisdiction in which I'm used to operating, we're always told to address the Bench rather than counsel, but I will adopt to the local procedure, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- it's good, therefore, that I raised the matter so that I understand. In this court it is quite common to address the examining counsel, and we have no problems in that. And if you would like to address the Court, now you have a problem, because there are two men and one woman, so "sir" would not do, "sirs" would not do, so perhaps it is an easy way out to address --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I appreciate that you are used to your own jurisdiction, and that's the problem everyone in this courtroom has already for some 13, 14 years. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Subject to the corrections which you set out in this document, does the content of the report that we saw on the screen accurately reflect your opinions and conclusions on the subject of the role of police and relationship with Knin garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender the public version of the report, which I mentioned is 2D00768; also the confidential version of the report, which is 2D00762, for the record; and, furthermore, so that it makes sense, the corrigendum which is 2D00788.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, in order to avoid that we have documents in evidence which do not add anything to other documents we have in evidence, the Chamber prefers to have the confidential version to be admitted into evidence, and then the public version could be filed as a document so that this -- so that it is accessible to the public, but that it's not evidence, only the confidential versions of these documents to be in evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report, which is 2D00762, becomes Exhibit D1776, under seal. And the corrigendum, which is 2D00788, becomes Exhibit D1777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1776 and D1777 are admitted into evidence. And the Cermak Defence is invited to file a public version of these documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, in addition to the report and the corrigendum, is it right that on Friday last week, you also prepared or, rather, during the course of last week you also prepared an additional note which was circulated to the Chamber and to the parties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly why it was that you prepared the note, and then outline the nature of its contents.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the note expands upon the section in my report which deals with the methodology of the preparation of the report, and the purpose of the additional note is to provide further transparency, further clarity to the Chamber on the way in which the report was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's not beyond dispute that it also contains a paragraph dealing with other issues arising from your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, there's a -- I beg your pardon. There's an update on my CV as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to start, before we go to the main report, by looking at what is Appendix 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We have no need to pull it up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I should say at the outset that I understand that you have a copy of the report before you, which is un-annotated. Is that right? In hard copy?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have a paper copy here which is straight out of the machine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also have two binders of documents which reflect the hard-copy content of your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, they were here in the building this morning, but I look in vain for them now, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Those can be provided to the witness, unless there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to start firstly with your CV and your experience as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the purposes of the Bench, I have discussed with Ms. Gustafson and it's appropriate that I lead this part of the evidence. If the Bench is satisfied. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Albiston, that after having served as a police officer in the UK and with the United Nations for a total of 28 years, you then since worked for a period of six years as a consultant in matters of policing, security, and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you began your career in 1975 with the London Metropolitan Police force and effectively worked your way up through the ranks, until in 1989, as I understand, you were transferred to the Royal Ulster Constabulary in Northern Ireland. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You have held various positions within the Royal Ulster Constabulary, including chief inspector, superintendent and chief superintendent until, in 1998, when you were appointed assistant chief constable.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now when you were first appointed assistant chief constable in the Royal Ulster Constabulary, could you expand upon what your initial duties were at that stage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. My first appointment was as the assistant chief constable responsible for a headquarters department called management support. That meant that I was responsible for all force policy, performance, research, communications, information technology, and various bits of a large organisation which didn't seem to fit anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: When did those duties change and what was the nature of that change?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: In September 1999, I was given an operational command, which made me the commander of what we called North Region which was an area of Northern Ireland in which I was responsible for all operational policing, the CID, special branch, uniform branch, and the support services.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in your position as assistant chief constable, is it right that you were responsible for commanding approximately 700 civilian staff, and over 3.000 police officers during a period of continued terrorism, public order problems and major police reform as taken from your CV. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And during that time, you were based in Belfast in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: My office was in Belfast. The area I was responsible for was quite extensive, stretching across the whole of the north and the west of the province.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You remained in that position until 2001, when you were seconded to the United Nations as the police commissioner for UNMIK, the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, which involved you commanding 4.500 international police officers from, I think, over 52 or around 52 different countries. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's right, ma'am. It fluctuated. It was usually 51 or 52 countries that were represented there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it also involved you developing the local force of approximately 4.500 officers at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: By the time I left Kosovo, the KPS, the Kosovo Police Service, numbered around 4 and a half thousand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now what was the nature, so that we understand, of your role in Kosovo as the police commissioner? What was your role and responsibilities at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, unusually for a United Nations policing mission, the United Nations police in Kosovo had an operational responsibility. That is to say, they actually delivered day-to-day policing services. It was not a monitoring mission or a training mission or an advisory mission; we were doing the policing work. At the same time, under the provisions of 1244 of 99, that's the United Nations authority, we were developing the local Kosovo police service with the eventual aim that they would replace the United Nations as the operational police for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now after a year serving in that position, you then returned to Belfast to your position as assistant chief constable for the crime department in the police service of Northern Ireland where you were responsible, as I understand, for all headquarter crime units and the special branch in Northern Ireland. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As an independent consultant thereafter for a period of six years, you have provided advice on policing, security, intelligence, risk management, and security sector reform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And during that time, the contracts that you undertook involved providing consultancy advice on policing matters to the Republic of Botswana, the Lithuanian Police Witness and Victim Protection Service and the Slovenian police service on leadership. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Those are some of the ones I dealt with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you have also been a consultant within police peacekeeping missions with the United Nations, the EU, and the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in the missions. I was providing training to officers preparing for leadership roles in those missions. That was with the police service of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And your consultancy has also extended to the Polish police service, the Slovak Ministry of Interior, the Estonian police service, and the British Home Office?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of your service as a professional police officer, it's right that you have received honours and awards which include the United Nations Civilian Police Medal in Kosovo 2001?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Officer of the Civil Division of the Order of the British Empire, OBE, 2001?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For services to policing. And Her Majesty The Queen's Golden Jubilee Medal in 2002?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the RUC George Cross Service Medal?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Having taken a whirlwind trip through your CV, Mr. Albiston, I would like to now -- again before we come to the meat of the report, I would like to ask you questions on the methodology and the way in which you prepared your report. Could you explain to the Chamber when you were asked to prepare a report in this case and by whom?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. As a result of a telephone conversation, I had a meeting with senior counsel in a hotel in Belfast in December 2007. Senior counsel being Mr. Kay. And Mr. Kay explained to me, in outline terms because we only had a three-hour meeting, what this case was about. He explained briefly the nature of the indictment in so far as it related to Mr. Ivan Cermak, and he explained briefly the grounds on which it was intended that Mr. Cermak would contest the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I was asked to consider assisting the Chamber as an expert witness by examining documents in relation to the case, in particular as they referred to Mr. Cermak's involvement with civilian policing, and to offer an opinion, based on my professional experience, in relation to those documents and to Mr. Cermak's criminal liability in relation to those specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you describe for us next how it was that you came to be provided with documents for you to consider in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. I received a large volume of documents from the Cermak Defence team, some in the form of hard paper copies in folders, and some in the form -- electronic form on discs, which I copied on to my own computer in order to read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Going into the layout of the report, can explain to us how you decided upon the layout and the presentation of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, the -- the form that the report takes now is a result of a changing, a developing process over many months. I read the documents and tried to make sense of them in the sense that I tried to order them in a way which was thematic. To some extent, this was done for me because some of the folders I received might be described as themed folders. Particular groups of documents were in particular folders. With other documents it was more difficult because the sheer mass of the material involved reading documents and trying to decide what, if anything, they referred to that was germane to my particular area of expertise. Gradually I started to group the ideas together, and then for the purposes of the report, I thought the best way to address it was to quote from parts of the indictment which were relevant to Mr. Cermak's relationship with civilian policing, and then address directly those issues on the basis of the documents which I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximation, if you can, of how many documents you reviewed in order to write this report, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, it would have to be an approximation. I would say it certainly exceeds 2.000 documents and probably doesn't exceed 4.000 documents. But it would be somewhere in that range.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could you explain for us how it was that you came to make your selection for the documents that you refer to in this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I tried to read most of the material that was provided to me. But sometimes I would find groups of documents which clearly all related to similar matters, which would be purely military, for example, and spent less time dealing with those. But I tried to read all the documents which I thought had some bearing on Mr. Cermak's dealings with the civilian police, or civilian policing issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: When did you submit your report to the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: The completed report was submitted towards the end of August of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you submit a draft report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I submitted a draft report in early May of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Are you able to explain how your report differed from your draft?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I made a number of changes after the draft was submitted, and I attempted to describe in summary form what these changes were in my additional note to which you referred at the earlier part of this -- this session. In summary, I cut out some bits of the report which, on reflection, may not have been so directly relevant to the areas in which I had expertise, and I tried to shorten and rearrange the report to bring greater focus and to make it more pertinent to the specific matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, in fact, some of the detail that you have referred to is contained in the additional note.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I hope the additional note makes it clear what the basic changes were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Albiston, did you type this report yourself or did somebody else perform that task?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I typed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you concluded writing your report, had you seen any other expert report in this trial?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I had seen the report by Mr. Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now there's one matter that I'd like to deal with, with you, which if we begin in the executive summary part of your report, you have the hard copy there, I don't think there's any need to pull it up onto the screen. But to assist my learned friend and the Chamber I'm going to be referring to paragraph 2.5 in your report which is on page 7 of the English, and for the purpose of the defendants, it is on page 7 of the Croatian version. If you can just get that paragraph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2.5, you have decided to look at staffing levels within the garrison. I wonder if could you explain for us why you chose to examine that, and you refer in particular to D992, D611, and D33, none of which I'd like to call up at this time. But could you give me your observations on the documents that you reviewed and why it was you decided to look at this issue, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. This was at a very early stage of my research. I was looking at strengths, because one of the matters which I felt I ought to consider was the span or breadth of command exercised by Mr. Cermak. And the documents appear to me to demonstrate that the garrison, the actual unit which Mr. Cermak commanded at the time, was in terms of numerical strength very small, and that the conclusion to be drawn from that was the function which he was exercising was an administrative function rather than an operational command, because 11 people is not -- are not going do achieve very much in operational terms in civilian policing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we can move on now to the next section of your report, which is on page 9 in the English. It's the section headed: Extent of the garrison commander's authority and responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have D1776, the report, on the screen at this stage, to help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to start off -- the section actually runs from paragraph 3.1 through to 3.9. And in paragraphs 3.1, you refer to the service regulations of the armed forces, which is D32. We see that reference there on the screen in front of us, where you've taken note of those particular regulations. It's a document which this Chamber is entirely familiar with, but to assist you, perhaps I could ask that D32 now be brought up onto the screen, please, at page 11 in the English, which is headed the section: Garrison, at paragraph 50. As that document is coming onto the screen, do you recall reviewing the service regulations, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you also recall reviewing an organisational order regarding work, order and discipline in the garrisons?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And for the record that is D34.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just waiting for D32 to come up onto the screen. What I'm going to ask you, Mr. Albiston, is, looking firstly at D32, the provisions relevant to the garrison, and thereafter, the organisational order, which we will look at in due course. I'm interested in what you were able to conclude from your review of these two documents, as to whether or not a garrison commander has any form of command or control over the civilian police, as reflected in these two documents. We're still waiting for, I think, paragraph 50 to come up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall the provisions --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I can answer your question. The purpose of looking at these two documents was to enable me to assess whether a garrison commander, in this time and this place, had any locus in civilian policing matters. It is clear from the documents that the function of the garrison commander is a military function, and not surprisingly from the language, it's a military appointment. But it would be quite possible for a military appointment or a function of this kind to have some sort of connection with civilian policing, so that is why I examined these two documents with some care, and the Chamber can see the conclusions which -- which I draw from my examination of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We see on the screen the section -- we see on the screen the section starting: "The garrison ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if we can go one page after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: These are the sections that have you looked at IN particular, as I understand, Mr. Albiston. Do you recall those provisions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do recall those provisions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like you now to briefly look at D34, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If that could be brought onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's the organisational order regarding work, order and discipline at garrison HQs, dated the 27th of August, 1993. And it's a document, again, that you cite in your report. As it's coming up, I would like you to pay particular attention, please, to paragraphs 2, 3, 4, and 5. And, again it's the same question: Whether or not this document assisted you in determining whether or not the garrison commander had any role of command or control over the civilian police as reflected in this particular document? Do you recall the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this document, and like the previous one, it enabled me to draw a conclusion that the garrison commander does not, in fact, have any function of command and control in relation to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, this document, D34, continues after the first two pages on the third page to go to instructions on regulating some issues within the jurisdiction of garrison headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we could bring up the third page, please, onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall this document, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I could ask for the next page to come up, please, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In paragraph 3.10 of your report, Mr. Albiston, which is page 12 in the English and the Croatian, you rely on paragraph 5 of the instruction. And, again, from your position as a professional police officer, can you assist us with how this provision is understood by you in terms of defining the garrison commander's relationship with the civilian police, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The document is quite clear in providing a role for the garrison commander, in relation to cooperation and coordination with the civilian police, not command or control over the civilian police. I read this document as a document which is really describing the functions of a garrison commander in peacetime, and these provisions, I think, are best interpreted in relation to the civilian police as a responsibility to conduct a liaison with the civilian police in order to prevent things like soldiers being rowdy on a Friday night. This is really what this is aimed at.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You've referred to -- this document, firstly, refers to the terms of cooperating and coordinating. You have referred also to the terms of command and/or control.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you deal briefly with this in section 3.12 of your report, which again is on page 12 in English and in Croatian. For the purposes of assisting this Chamber, could you briefly outline for us, from your perspective, again, as a professional police officer, the meaning, as you understand those terms, on the one hand, coordination and cooperation; on the other hand, command and control, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. For the police, command and control indicates a responsibility so that command is a function of an individual, an individual who gives orders, directions, sets policy, provides leadership, and who expects, in return, that those orders should be followed and obeyed. He expects reports back on the way in which the commands have been carried out. Control nowadays is very often used to refer to the mechanisms, if I can put it that way, by which command is exercised. And, in particular, police and to some extent soldiers talk about command and control and think about control rooms with banks of computer screens and -- and telecommunications equipment and this sort of thing, but control can also be the chain of command through which orders are passed down, and reports and responses are passed back. So command and control are terms with different meanings but which are both common to a hierarchical system of instructions and directions. Cooperation and coordination are very different. Cooperation in the civilian policing context can be understood in the ordinary use of the word "cooperation." It's different groups coming together for a common purpose. It may be different organisations coming together for a common purpose, and the organisations may not have overall shared agendas, but in relation to the matters on which they cooperate, they do find common ground. Coordination, particularly in policing and military terms, is not just the ordinary use of the noun to do things together and to avoid duplication, but in policing and military circles it has the additional connotation of trying to avoid what, in some places, is referred to as a blue-on-blue incident. In other words, the compromise of an operation, because different elements who are expected to cooperate together have not communicated properly. They have not established their different area of responsibilities properly and so on. So that would be coordination in a policing sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Another tranche of evidence that you review, or documentation, refers to the structure of the Ministry of the Interior, and you deal with that in the next section on page 13 which is entitled: Police Structures and the Croatian Ministry of the Interior. In that section, again, to summarise, you refer to documents which include the Law on Internal Affairs, D1077; the Law on Amendments to the Law on Internal Affairs, P1148; the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, 65 ter 1810; the Decree on Internal Organisation and Operation of the Ministry of Interior, 65 ter 6104; and the Decree on Seats and Areas of Police Administrations, D443. You also include a document - which I'd like to have on the screen, please - which is P6 -- sorry, P962, which is a document exhibited in this trial, showing the organigram effectively of the Ministry of Interior in Croatia at the relevant time. Now having conducted the review as you have, as that document is coming onto your screen, from paragraphs 3.15 in your report through to 3.23, you have considered the bare bones and the documentation that go to those bones of the structure from the level, as we see on the screen, of the minister of the interior, to the assistant ministers, the chiefs of sectors, the police administrations, and the police stations. Now, Mr. Albiston, at the end of your section which deals with the Ministry of the Interior, you make the conclusion that the garrison commander had no role to play within the structure of the Ministry of the Interior, and that conclusion is in paragraph 3.19 of your report. Do you recall this section of the report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The previous section, I looked at the role of the garrison commander to see whether there was any connection between that function and civilian policing; and in this section, I looked at the other side of the equation, the Ministry of the Interior and the civilian policing, to see whether there was any locus within that structure for the garrison commander. And after examining these documents carefully, both in terms of the structures, the organigrams and so on, as well as looking at the named individuals, there was no mention of a garrison commander in any of these Ministry of the Interior and civilian policing structures, and there's no mention of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in examining the particularities of the Ministry of the Interior within Croatia, you noted or took note of the different police administrations; for example, the Kotar-Knin police administration and the Zadar-Knin police administration. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I please have on the screen D442.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now what's coming up, Mr. Albiston, is a map which has been exhibited, entitled: The area of the municipalities of Kotar district Knin police administration. And I'd like you to look at this map, and a second map in turn, because one of the conclusions that you reach, or one of your observations in paragraph 3.19 of your report is the following.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And that is on page 15 for everybody's purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It should be noted that territorially, much of the Knin-Kotar police administration lay outside the Knin garrison command. Now, firstly I'd like you to look at this map so that we understand the different geographical layouts. And if you could give me your observations on this map first, please, in terms of the garrison and the conclusion that you made.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. The garrison area tends to be a relatively small part of the shaded area down to the -- to the south and east of the shaded area of the map, or the bottom right-hand side, for those who don't like south and east orientations. Significantly, more than half the shaded area is outside the Knin garrison area. Now, one of the implications of that, for those from a police or military background, is the concept of the territorial area of responsibility, and I'm sure the Chamber will be aware that if they go into a -- a policeman's office or a soldiers barracks, they're likely to see maps on the walls. This is quite a common feature, and that is because as policemen, certainly, I can't speak for the military, but as police officers we're very concerned about maps and where our responsibility starts and finishes. And I drew attention of the Chamber in my report to the fact that the Knin garrison area is, by no means, coterminous with the Kotar-Knin police administration area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to see if we can assist you further by pulling onto the screen, please, 2D00789.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And for the purposes of my learned friend and the Chamber, what is coming up is a map that has been prepared by the Zagreb Cermak Defence team, which Mr. Albiston had a chance to review yesterday. We hope that it will be of some assistance to the Chamber as it contains ten-kilometre buffer zones, so it is an easier reckoner in terms of the distance that apply throughout the administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, could you take a look at this map, please, which, as can you see, indicates Knin as a town, the municipalities are named surrounding Knin; Kotar-Knin police administration, with the number of kilometres calculated; and also Zadar-Knin police administration. Now, what observations do you have, from your perspective again as a professional police officer, in terms of the areas that we're looking at here, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think the first observation to make is that the geographical area covered by the Kotar-Knin police administration is large. The distance from the town of Knin to some of the areas in the north of the police administration area is up to 100 kilometres. And this, from a policing perspective, presents certain difficulties, in terms of covering areas effectively. From a uniform policing point of view, the difficulties are the sheer size of the area, so that in order to maintain a visible uniform police presence and to carry out effective patrolling, the number of officers required would be quite considerable, because of the area, the length of the road, the distances to travel, the number of potential road crossing points, and so on. Additionally, from the policing perspective, if we look at the criminal investigation side of policing responsibilities, distances to be travelled can impact on the quality of criminal investigations. And I mention that because if we look at the map that's on the screen now, we can see that for some parts of the Kotar-Knin police administration area, the distance from the town of Knin and the distance from the town of Zadar is probably not significantly different, if you look, for example, at the areas in the far north. If, however, you look at the areas of the greater population concentration within the Zadar-Knin police administration, you will see that for most of those areas Zadar is significantly further away than the town of Knin itself. Now, that is not surprising. But the difficulty that this creates is that my examination of the documents suggests that the -- for the main part, the resources of the criminal investigation department, or the crime police of the civilian police, were centred on Zadar, and that, with the exception of an individual gentleman called Mr. Krvavica and subsequently five additional officials, the centre from which crime police officers would operate in relation to serious crimes committed in the Kotar-Knin police administration was, in fact, Zadar. And there are reasons why I think this would be problematic. Firstly, there is the traditional problem that police from outside an area have less of a feel for the population with which they're dealing. Sometimes that doesn't matter; sometimes it does. Sometimes police are able to get more information or understand more effectively the information which they do receive, if they have a greater contact, a greater level of understanding of the local community. So distance would be a problem there. But distance is also a problem from the technical perspective of a modern crime investigation. There are problems with not getting to a scene quickly, in relation to potential forensic evidence. If you don't get to a crime scene quickly, you may not see the crime scene in the condition in which it was when the crime took place. Obviously the sooner you get there, the more like the scene at the time of the crime you will see. This is useful, for example, for obtaining photography of crime scenes. It is useful for gauging what the light conditions were or what the weather conditions were at the time of a major crime. It's useful for the apprehension of offenders. It may seem an obvious point, but the longer you take to get to the crime scene, the more opportunity offenders have to escape. But it goes more -- more deeper than that, because the longer it takes you to get to a crime scene with your team of investigators, the less chance of getting witnesses who were present at the time of the events. You may not be able to be so precise about when the incident did occur, if you takes you a long time to get to the crime scene. So there are all sorts of reasons why I thought it worth mentioning in my report that whilst we have the existence of the Kotar-Knin police administration set up under the laws of the Republic of Croatia for the reasons which are given in the report, in relation to the special legislation on the protection of minorities, there was, in my view, as police officer, a disadvantage in having resources for criminal investigation for serious crime centred outside the police administration area itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Albiston. In fact you deal with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. Mr. Albiston - and I'm referring to page 26, line 3 and following - you said: "If, however, you look at the areas of the greater population concentration within the Zadar-Knin police administration, you will see that for most of those areas Zadar is significantly further away than the town of Knin itself." What did you consider to be the greater population concentration? Could you just explain on the basis of this map, point at a certain place of greater population concentration, where we would see that Zadar is significantly further away than the town of Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I appreciate that the map is not marked according to population density. But I have seen other maps which have towns with marks on the towns to show the size of the population. And my recollection is that if you look at the map which is currently displayed, you will see that there is a pale yellow colour which indicates a lowland or valley, and my recollection is that there were more -- there was a greater concentration of population in those areas than in the darker shaded areas which represent hilly or mountainous terrain. So what -- the point that I was making was that in the north of the Kotar-Knin police administration, probably the distances between individual villages and the town of Knin or individual villages and the town of Zadar is not significant, but in the southern part of the Kotar-Knin police administration area, it becomes apparent that Knin is closer to those population centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your answer you referred to the Zadar-Knin police administration, which I expected to be the blue part of this map. The examples you are now giving are about the Kotar-Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you referring to areas of greater population in the area we find described as the Kotar-Knin police administration on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. President, if I didn't make clear, I was referring only in my answer about population to the Kotar-Knin administration area in yellow on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And not the blue area of Zadar-Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the expression Zadar-Knin police administration and we were looking at this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, well, then I apologise for my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is there a term that are you familiar with or that you use to refer to the time immediately after a crime has been committed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. In some policing circles in the English-speaking world, the expression "golden hour" is used and that is particularly a reference to apprehension of offenders, the collection or identification of witnesses, and specifically the opportunities to capture forensic material at a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this map. I understand that it was provided to Ms. Gustafson, I think, yesterday. Of course, she may need some time to verify that. But I would seek to tend it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could just have a day or so to compare it with our information. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you assign an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1778, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now if we proceed through your report, I'm going to be dealing with page 19 next, and paragraph 3.33 --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Which for everyone's purposes is, in fact, still page 19 in the Croatian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In this section --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And could I ask for D589 to be brought up onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In this section of your report, you draw conclusions about the position of the higher echelons of the police towards Mr. Cermak, and you rely upon a report prepared by Senior Police Coordinator Tomurad for the attention of Assistant Minister Moric, dated the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You see on the screen there, the front page of the document, dated the 28th of August, and the part that you rely on in your report is, in fact, found on page 2 of that document. And it's at the bottom in the English, which begins: "I also deem it necessary to achieve an agreement ..." Do you see that part of the text?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I recall this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you if you can explain, please, in further detail why it is that you attribute importance to this document in revealing the relationship between the higher echelons of the MUP, as you refer to them, and Mr. Cermak, in terms of the relationship of policing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I think this document is particularly significant for two reasons. One reason is that having examined many, many documents, internal documents in the Ministry of the Interior, and in civilian policing, without finding any reference whatsoever to General Cermak or the garrison commander, I now have this document which talks about issues relating to civilian policing, and it does mention General Cermak. And what it says is, as you quoted, that it would be useful for representatives to be in Mr. Cermak's meetings. And to me the significance of that is that if General Cermak, as garrison commander, featured in any way in the Ministry of the Interior or civilian policing hierarchy, surely there would be no need to ask for civilian police officers to be present in meetings which he chaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you go on, leaving this document aside, to refer to other documents in paragraphs 3.34, 3.35, and 3.36 of your report, which are pages 19 to 20, where you conclude that Mr. Cermak did not have legal authority over the police, having reviewed both MUP documents, in the preparation of your report, and the testimony of several witnesses, which you cite in your report, and I'm not going to take you through all of those documents. But I do have this question for you, Mr. Albiston, which is in fact the reverse, the opposite of what you have been doing. If Mr. Cermak was in command and/or control of the civilian police, what would you have expected to have seen within the MUP documentation which you reviewed, given your experience in numerous policing systems to have shown that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I would expect General Cermak's name to appear on a significant array of documents of different types. For example, I would expect to see his name on instructions, policy documents, orders going out to the civilian police. I would expect to see his name on orders transferring or appointing senior police officers. I would expect to see his name on reports going up the Ministry of the Interior chain of command for the information of senior personnel in Zagreb. There are many documents in which I would expect to find his name, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, just going back to the previous document which we looked at, which is still on your screen, this is D589, which reads -- in your answer that you gave to us, you stated: "And to me the significance of that is if General Cermak, as garrison commander, featured any way in the Ministry of Interior or civilian policing hierarchy, surely there would be no need to ask for civilian police officers to be present in meetings which he chaired." If we go back to look at the text of that, it refers to General Cermak holding meetings with UNCRO, UNCIVPOL and other international organisations in Knin. It doesn't to refer to him chairing meetings. It refers to the police wanting to be present at the meetings which he held. Could you assist me with the statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I am aware that --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I'm aware that he held meetings. If he held meetings, it may be an assumption or it may be a correct assumption to say that he chaired the meetings which he held. But I accept that, on this particular script, the words are "meetings that General Cermak holds with members of the UN mission." It's a recognition of his international liaison function.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you on to page 21 of your report, please, and the section which is headed: The garrison commander's relationship with the civilian police, just to explore there further. At the start of that section you examine the allegation contained in paragraph 19 of the indictment, which is set out at the top of the page, referring to Mr. Cermak directing, facilitating, supporting, and issuing orders to elements and/or members of the HV and RH MUP, including the military and civilian police. Do you recall that allegation that you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the conclusion that you make differs from that conclusion, or rather, differs from the indictment that we see at the top of the page. In your section of the opinion and your report, you conclude that the relationship that Mr. Cermak had with the civilian police was one of cooperation. And I'd like to examine that a little bit further and why it is you come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: There's a document that I would like you to look at which is a document under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So if could not be brought up onto the public monitors. It's D487, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it's a document which you cite, Mr. Albiston, at paragraph 3.38, page 21 in Croatian. And it will come up on your screen to assist you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, we can safely deal with this document without going into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my estimation is that we can. Mr. Albiston is aware of the meaning of under seal documents and I hope that he will be able to deal with that appropriately. Yes, is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Given the proviso that I have stated that this document is under seal, and if there's any moment where you feel further explanation would be needed, please tell me so that we can go into private session. Could you explain, please, the basis of why it is you rely on this document to explain the relationship between Mr. Cermak and the civilian police, as one of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. This -- this document is providing information to General Cermak. The local police chief has provided this information in relation to a crime matter. But he hasn't responded to an order down a chain of command. The introductory paragraph states: "On the basis of your verbal request for a statement ..." To me, as a police officer, senior police officers may make verbal requests to junior police officers, but they wouldn't see that request described as a verbal request in a written document which came by way of reply. This is indicative of someone from outside a hierarchy, seeking the assistance of someone who is inside the hierarchy. And it goes on to say: "... a verbal request which was made to you by international institutions ..." And I think from that we are entitled to conclude that the author of this document is saying to General Cermak, Well, look, I understand that you have a liaison function with the internationals, and you've asked me for some information in relation to a crime matter because those internationals have made a request to you, so here is some basic information. And furthermore, if we look at the final paragraph, we see that the police chief is saying, And by the way, I haven't got authority to give you some information in relation to other matters. Now, I have worked in different areas of policing, and I have worked in areas in which information, shall we say, is restricted, and sometimes there are caveats put on information that it cannot be transmitted without special authority, but that has never applied in an upwards direction in a direct hierarchical situation. There is not a situation in policing where you cannot tell your immediate superior some information because he is not entitled to know it or that you don't have authority to give that information to that individual. That does not take place in a police hierarchy. So I think, if you look at the totality of the two points from the first paragraph and the final paragraph, the conclusion that you have to draw from this document is that General Cermak was not within the civilian police -- policing hierarchy, and that the author of this document certainly did not believe him to be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be moving to another document. I don't know whether it's an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Ms. Higgins. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, when I invited the Cermak Defence to file the public version of the report, you were kind enough not to tell me that I had forgotten that it was filed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, there is no need to do that, and apologies for the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I have a note to remind myself to the same effect so ... it's on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, we left just before the break looking at your conclusions in terms of the relationship of cooperation between Mr. Cermak and the civilian police. And I want to look at some of the other documents that you rely on in support.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I ask that document P2649 be brought onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One of the platforms of documentation that you rely on in making that conclusion is the document that Mr. Cermak was receiving from the police. And I'd like to take now -- look now at the documents in turn, three of them. The first which is coming on to the screen, P2649, and this is a document from Ivica Cetina, dated the 10th of October, 1995, to the Knin garrison headquarters, attention General Cermak. Do you recall this document that you relied on, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could you tell me why you relied on it in support of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. If we examine the document, we see that it refers to a number of incidents in which the civilian police have been involved, and the information regarding these incidents is coming from Mr. Cetina, a police -- civilian police chief, and the memorandum is addressed to the Knin garrison for the attention of General Cermak. And I think it is particularly worth noting, the first line of the first paragraph which explains the circumstances under which Mr. Cetina, from within the civilian policing hierarchy, is providing information to General Cermak, who is not, in my submission, within the civilian police hierarchy. And that is that the -- the communication says: "In reply to the request of the International Red Cross organisation for submission of data on ... incidents that occurred in the area of Knin ..." So my conclusion is that this document reinforces the view that the civilian police recognised that General Cermak had a role in relation to the international community, in this case, the ICRC, and that they were assisting General Cermak to carry out his role by providing information which that international body had requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document in turn that you rely on is P2650, and that is a document which is dated the 11th of October, again, sent to the Knin garrison for General Cermak, signed by Chief Cetina, we can see, on the Croatian version there at the bottom. And again, it's a document that you rely on to support your conclusion, Mr. Albiston. If we take a look firstly at the first page, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if we just scan, please, to the second page so that you've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, again, same question: Could you assist me as to why it is you have relied on this document, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, well, I think we can see by looking at a combination of the English translation and the original document that this, as you say, from Chief Cetina, and it's information being supplied again to the Knin garrison for the information of the garrison commander, General Cermak. And it amounts to very brief rehearsal of information, in relation to the killing of three people, and informs the General that the correct investigative and judicial procedure has been initiated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And onto the third document in line, please, which is 2645, P2645.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is an document dated the 21st of October, 1995, coming from Zvonko Gambiroza, station commander, and it's to the attention there to various police divisions and authorities. And also you see Knin command post headquarters, attention of General Cermak. The front page is on the screen before you. And it's a subject relating to plaintiff Luka Pasic, criminal act of aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we could ask for the second page to be put onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, in order to assist, this may give you some detail as to help with your recollection of what we're talking about here. You see an outline of the crime itself and the location within the village of Oton Bender. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And can you assist again with why it is you've relied upon this document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I have to say at the outset that the provenance of this document is not entirely clear to me, or should I say the purpose of the document is not entirely clear to me. But I think it's interesting because of the large number of recipients and the information which is supplied in it, which, whilst it is not in the format that you might expect for a detailed description of an incident, an investigation being passed between police officers, it nevertheless provides significantly more information than, for example, the previous document, which I was shown just now. The other recipients are police, and it refers to a crime matter. I think what is quite clear is that because of the recipients and the way that the paper is addressed, there's no expectation of any action on the part of General Cermak in response to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I'd like to take you on to a point that you make now in paragraph 3.40 of your report, which you will find at page 22 in both the Croatian and the English versions. And it's the point that you make that correspondence initiated by Mr. Cermak with the MUP tended to be in relation to administrative matters, such as accommodation, and did not concern operational policing matters. Do you have that part of the report before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I would like to you explain, please, the term "operational policing matters" and what it means to you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's quite a -- an understood concept within policing circles that there is operational policing, and that there is non-operational or administrative support, and I think the functions are quite distinct and quite well understood by police. So, for example, operational matters would include police patrols, guarding duties, check-points, investigations, public order duties, checks on borders, anything in which the police are doing what only the police can do. Very often in contact with the public. Sometimes in contact with other agencies but certainly designed to achieve policing objectives. Administrative matters are those matters which any large organisation has to engage in, in order to function effectively, and that could include recruitment and selection procedures, training, promotion, internal discipline, policy setting, things like that. That's what I distinguish. So, for example, if you were sending police officers to carry out a patrol or to set up a check-point, that would be a operational matter. If you were allocated housing or refreshment allowances for police officers, that would be an administrative matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in the documents that you -- in the documents that you reviewed, and you've told us the extent of that documentation, did you see any documents from or to Mr. Cermak which you would consider to be operational policing matters?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: There were documents which could be said to impact on operational policing matters. In particular, I have in mind in answer to that question, documents concerning missing United Nations vehicles and equipment. The majority of documents which I saw in relation to matters which might impact upon policing which General Cermak was involved in or Ministry of the Interior correspondence, were simply administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I will be coming on to deal with the UN vehicles so we'll deal with that at a later point.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now you also refer to matters of cooperation within the Ministry of the Interior, between Assistant Minister Moric and Mate Lausic, commander of the VP administration? Do you recall that section?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, can I take you, please, so you have it before you, to paragraph 3.42 of your report, which you will find on page 23. And, in particular, I'm interested in footnote 75, which provides the base for your conclusions that you make, as to the cooperation between the two bodies. I'd like to pull up a few examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we could start with first, please, D269.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, I'm going to ask you why it is you rely and why it is you consider these documents to be relevant in establishing the relationship that existed, firstly, between the civilian police and the military police; and secondly, whether there is anything you would wish to observe in relation to the role of Mr. Cermak. Is that clear, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we turn firstly, then, to D269.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And as it is coming up on the screen, again, this is a document dated the 3rd of August, 1995, and it's a document, the subject of which is: Order on the work of the military police, cooperation between joint work of the civilian and military police, and obligations of the military police towards detained members of paramilitary and para-police formations. Does this document look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we can scan perhaps to the last page of that document. It's a three-page document --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So that you've seen the reference there to Mate Lausic and the individuals to whom it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the content of that order is, in fact, referred to on page 2, just again so that you have seen it to refresh your memory --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If that is brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So that you can see what was being ordered in respect of that cooperation, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you assist me as to why it was you selected this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: To me, it indicated the preparations which were being made by the Ministry of Defence, the military police section, for the aftermath of Operation Storm, and the recognition that there would be a need for cooperation between the Ministry of Defence, in the form of the military police, and the Ministry of the Interior, in the form of the civilian police, in order to achieve government objectives in relation to the maintenance of law and order in the area after the military operation. And I think the significance for this Chamber, in relation to General Cermak, is that whilst in many aspects he was regarded as a focal point for cooperation and coordination, when we look at the detail of the operational responsibilities of the civilian police, and, indeed, in this case, the military police, we find no locus for General Cermak or the garrison commander whatsoever. This was an operational matter and he does not appear to have any role in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's look further in time. If we looked now to D46, which takes us to the 10th of August, and it's a document from Josko Moric, the assistant minister of the interior, to Chief Major-General Mate Lausic. And I'd like you to take a look. There are three paragraphs in the document, if you remind yourself of its content, and, again, its significance, please, to your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. This is the -- the other side of the equation, so to speak. Mr. Moric, who was one of the addressees of the previous document, is here sending a communication to his opposite number, and the significance is that it refers to the continuing need for cooperation between the civilian police and the military police. In particular, in this instance, Mr. Moric is addressing two problems. One is that the need for the joint roadblocks and so on, and the other is he is drawing attention to the possibility that persons who are either members of the Croatian Army or at least persons in Croatian Army uniforms are involved in criminal acts, and that under the provisions of the law it would be necessary for the military police to assist the civilian police in dealing with that particular issue. And, of course, although this is a cooperation and coordination issue, because it is operational, General Cermak doesn't feature anywhere in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next example from your footnote that I would like you to take a look at, please, is D48. And, again, moving forward in time a week to the 17th of August now, it will be a document from Josko Moric, again, for the attention of Mr. Lausic. It's a two-page document reflecting communication between the two parties. If could you take a look firstly at the front page to refamiliarise yourself. And, again, the same question, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And onto page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. The -- this note, a week after the previous one, rehearses the same concerns and suggests that, in fact, the objectives which were sought to be achieved by the previous letter have not in fact been achieved. And Mr. Moric is exhorting Major-General Lausic to greater efforts by his people to ensure that this cam be improved. Once again, I see no reference to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One final document in the series from that footnote 75, which is D586, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, we move forward in time, Mr. Albiston, to the 22nd of August, correspondence from Josko Moric to Chief Lausic, relating to matters of cooperation between the civilian and the military police at this stage of events. I'm going to ask you to look briefly at the front page to ensure that you recall the document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And on the second page, you will see there, second paragraph: "Measures that are proposed in relation to reducing to potential problems through cooperated actions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, finally, the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Where there is reference to the proposal to a meeting to discuss the situation in the field. And this is the last in the series that I will take you to. And it's the same question as before, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, the themes are similar. There's an additional matter which is raised here by the author of the document, which is the concern that demobilisation will lead do what the author calls materiel, weapons, ordnance and such-like, being at liberty in the area and that it's necessary for the civilian police and the military police to cooperate in order to mitigate any difficulties which might arise from that situation, and it calls for a meeting.
