There were, of course, meetings at all levels between the military police and the civilian police to discuss arrangements for handling these problems, and in none of those meetings and in none of this correspondence is there any reference to the garrison commander, General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now following on from these documents, on a similar but related theme, you go on at page 24 of your report to deal with the allegation of the garrison commander as a superior of the civilian police. And I'm interested, in particular, if we start at paragraph 3.47, as part of the review that you undertook for this section, from reading your report, we can see that you looked at the directive governing the internal structure of the Ministry of the Interior, which is D527. Was there anything in that legislation that would support that particular allegation, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Not at all, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's a document that you're familiar with --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- so I don't intend do bring it back onto the screen. Now in the following paragraph, 3.48, you observe that documents in this case demonstrate that General Cermak was not within the MUP chain of reporting and command, and in particular the documents in support in footnote 93. And what I'd like to do is to pull up several examples from that reference and to ask you about the nature of the documents that you reviewed --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- and why it is you came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first document being, please, D498.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And this document is dated the 24th of August, 1995, a document from Chief Cetina to the Ministry of the Interior, assistant minister, and, again, in paragraph two, as it is coming up, there's reference to matters of cooperation. So an internal MUP document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sorry, I've made a mistake. Could I ask for P498. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, if could you just confirm, when it comes on your screen, that it's a document that you recall. And then I'd like your observations, Mr. Albiston, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I recall --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Does that look familiar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I recall this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if we could go onto page 2, which contains more of the substance of the document itself. And if would you take it from me that it's signed by Ivica Cetina, it's not in dispute, then perhaps you could assist us with why it is you've selected this document, bearing in mind the theme of your chapter here which is the allegation of Mr. Cermak as a superior of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, this document shows the conduct of police operations and it takes the form of a report on progress in a number of matters and gives some information about what the police have actually done. The civilian police, that is. Although it also refers to the cooperation with the military police. But in relation to these matters, the report is going through Ministry of the Interior reporting channels and not to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document -- Your Honour, this a document under seal, which is P499. Again I'm confident that it can be dealt with with the witness without going into private session, but for the purpose of the Registry, if could not appear on public screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your cautious approach is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, again, with the proviso of an approach of care with this document, could you explain to us the basis of your reasoning for including it in this section.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I could see the second page, please. Yes, again, this is a police document. The author is informing the addressee of the actions taken by the civilian police to address some of the problems which were occurring in his particular area of command, which is within the area which we're discussing today. And it is an internal civilian police, Ministry of the Interior document, which makes no reference to the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to cut short my reliance on other documents and just call up two more which you rely on in this section.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the first is D573, D573, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 24th of August, and it's a document sent by chief of the PU, Drago Matic, to the Ministry of the Interior, reference: As regards your telegram number and reference there to the state of cooperation in paragraph 1, as it comes up before you. Is that a familiar document, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if we could have --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So that you have seen it again --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's another document which is consistent with a great many that I reviewed, which show internal police reports going through an internal civilian police reporting structure, as would be expected in a hierarchy, within the Ministry of the Interior. And like so many of these reports, a considerable number that I reviewed, there are elements of cooperation between different state agencies mentioned; for example, cooperation between the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior, in relation to the working practices between the civilian police and the military police. But although General Cermak has a coordinating role in this area, he doesn't get a mention. He doesn't get a copy of the documents. And I think the inference, the conclusion which can be drawn from all these documents is that when it comes to operational matters, General Cermak didn't have a role to play.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The last document which I'm going to take you to from your footnote is D574, please. And this is a document dated the 30th of August, 1995, from Josko Moric to the police administrations listed. And in it, he refers to the fact that: "We requested a report on linkage with the military police in order to prevent further torching of houses and illegal taking of movable property from rightful owners." That's on the first page before you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the second page, please, you see Josko Moric is writing about the responses he received to date.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, again, this is another document you rely on in the series to support your conclusion that Mr. Cermak was a superior to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Certainly. And I think one of the things about this particular document is that in two places there's a hint or suggestion of irritation or at least an indication that Mr. Moric isn't satisfied with the service which is being provided. And you might expect that if General Cermak featured anywhere within the Ministry of the Interior hierarchy, and Mr. Moric, as the assistant minister, were not satisfied with the completeness or timeliness of the reports he were receiving from junior officers within that hierarchy, that he might seek to invoke the assistance of General Cermak. But he doesn't, and he doesn't because General Cermak is not part of this hierarchical structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I take you now to the next page of your report, please, which is page 26 in the English, and page 26 and 27 in the Croatian. And I'm interested in paragraphs 3.50 through to 3.52, where you consider, again within this same section of whether or not Mr. Cermak was a superior to the civilian police, you consider the issue of passes. And I'd like to take you through a series of documents and, again, all of these are referenced in your report, and to seek your observations in respect thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first document I'd like on the screen, please, is P493.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it's a document which is dated the 3rd of August, 1995, from Josko Moric to the following police administrations which are listed, headed: Cooperation with military police. I'd like you to read carefully. Point 1 refers to several points of the order. And, in particular, the point about the pass which is mentioned there. Do you see any reference there to the -- to passes --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, the third bullet point in paragraph 1 refers to passes which have been signed jointly by General Tolj and Colonel Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. And just for the record, it refers to journalists, foreign statesmen and so on can enter the liberated territory through the said check-points in the operations area only by producing a pass, signed jointly by Tolj and Rebic. We're going through this because it becomes relevant to other documents that you referred to, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document I would like, please, is D1014. Moving forward in time five days to the 8th of August, 1995. And the document which will come on your screen is a document from Ivo Cipci which he sends to the Ministry of Interior operative headquarters, and he is requesting an opinion in this document, four lines of text. And I'd just like you to remind yourself, please, of the content of that document and its significance to your report, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. This is a civilian police chief seeking the advice of the Ministry of Interior on the question of passes and free movement for citizens in the relevant area, because he is unsure what steps to take and what the regulations are. So he doesn't ask the garrison commander in Knin. He asks the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And a document of the same date, of D1769, please, on the 8th of August. It's a two-page document from Josko Moric to the police administrations which are listed. And it concerns the arrival of reporters and public figures in the liberated area, and it addresses some of the procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, what I'm interested in, Mr. Albiston, is why you considered this to be relevant to your report, please. Does this look familiar, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if we could have page 2, please, of the English on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, if you could assist me as to why you have relied on this report in this section.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, it's not entirely clear to me whether this is a response on the same day to the previous inquiry, but whether or not that is the case, it certainly addresses the same issue, and it makes it clear that the Ministry of the Interior is the body which has the authority for dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D494, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. It's just not clear to me where this document is relied on in the report, and perhaps counsel could assist me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: My apologies, I actually think Ms. Gustafson is correct, that this is a document that was not relied upon in the report, and I will verify that. But it is a document that I would like Mr. Albiston to have seen and I know that he has seen, and therefore I would like his observations as he has given them, unless there is any objection in relation thereto. So if could I put that point on the record and I will verify it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, so the question would then be a different one, would you have relied on this document if --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or whether he did not include that, if it is not to be found in the footnotes, rather than to ask him why he relied upon it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have a moment to verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, in relation to this document, this is a document that I asked to you comment on, had you seen this document before I asked you about it? Because it is not contained in your report, in fact.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, it certainly looks familiar. Does it have a number in the court systems, the Chamber's accounting system?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The only number that it has is the ERN number at the top of the document on the first page, and it also has D1769, which is an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An exhibit number, I take it, that was assigned after the report was produced, in view of the number itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can tell the Chamber that the document looks familiar. I can also tell the Chamber that I examined a significant number of 0361 documents. I cannot be precise and say to the Chamber, yes, this document is one that I have read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you been provided with documents after you had produced the report in its final version or after had you produced the draft report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen documents which have a new number, because they have been entered into the court system or exhibited in the Chamber subsequent to my considering them. I'm -- I'm not sure whether that -- whether they're always documents which I haven't seen before. Some of them, I think, I have seen before in a previous system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document which is contained in your report is D494, please. And this is a document from Ivo Cipci, dated the 15th of August, 1995. And it refers to the submission of a pass for entering the Knin garrison, issued by the HV command, and asking for a reply and confirmation in writing as to the validity of the passes for civilian persons in question. And you see at the bottom it also has some handwriting that has been typed out onto the document for our purposes. Do you recollect that document, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And why is it you considered that to be of particular relevance to this section?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think if we read the text of the document and the handwritten note in translation, the implication is that the officials of the Ministry of the Interior did not believe that General Cermak had authority to issue passes or to deal with this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd to look a document that is related to this document, which is in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I would like to look at a document which is related to this document, which is, in fact, D495. And if I could ask that the English version be put on the screen first, please, which may speed up the questioning to some extent, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it's in fact the document which is attached to the one we've just seen, the submission of the pass, the permit to enter the garrison. And, again, you will see some handwriting on the bottom of the document, which I'd like to you look at, and observe as to why you understood this document to be of relevance to your section, please, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, part of the delay is my eyes are at the stage where they have difficulty with the screen, either the writing is too far away or the glasses aren't working properly. But it's clear that this -- this deals with the same issue and indicates the understanding and the -- that General Cermak's passes were not recognised by the Ministry of the Interior as having validity for persons other than military personnel or civilians working within the military establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And what observations do you make in regards to Mr. Cermak's authority in this respect?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, the clear inference from these documents is that so far as the people in the Ministry of the Interior were concerned, General Cermak didn't have that authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document, please, is D496.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And this is dated 15th of August, from Ivo Cipci to the Ministry of the Interior. Subject: Visits and admission to the liberated areas. It's a document that you rely on in your report. And it refers to the text of: "We are very pressured by citizens and displaced persons who wish to visit the liberated areas, Knin, Drnis," et cetera. Is this a document you recall, firstly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like you to see, as well, the second page, and look at the text on that page, which gives a context to what Mr. Cipci is asking for.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, it's a civilian police official seeking guidance from the Ministry of the Interior. In other words, it's a transaction which is taking place within the Ministry of the Interior hierarchy, concerning the free movement of citizens and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, let's look at P509, please, now, which is a document which comes from General Cermak. And it is a document entitled: Order, dated the 15th of August, 1995. Paragraphs 1 and 2. Paragraph 2 referring to: "... permit civilians to enter the town of Knin without passes, and carry out routine checks following the rules set out earlier." Document you rely on, a document you cite, what are your observations in relation to this document, which does come from Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, in this -- in this document, General Cermak is giving permission or agreeing that people can move freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you have any other observations about it in relation to the authority of Mr. Cermak, in respect of the documents that we've seen preceding it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- it's -- you could say it is consistent with those documents in that, on that this date, General Cermak is not seeking to exercise authority or restrict freedom of movement of citizens in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The last document is P510, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is a document dated 16th of August --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. That document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which requires the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- cautious approach.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Ms. Gustafson, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Document dated 16th of August. I'd like you to consider, in particular, the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise again for the interruption. This document is not referenced in the witness's report and I'm wondering if a foundation could be laid as to the witness's knowledge of the document before further questions are asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I will, of course, do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you could JUST read through that text, Mr. Albiston --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it a document that you have seen before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you help us with any observations that you may have in respect of this document, given what you know in terms of the documentation you have reviewed? And if there's a need for us to go into private session --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- please indicate if you would feel that it would better express your views, we would be able to do.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I will try to deal with this question without that requirement. This document represents the transmission of the views of General Cermak, as we saw in the previous document, into the context of the civilian policing chain of command, and my interpretation of this document is that the author is transmitting that information to the heads of the police stations within the Kotar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the next collection you examine are passes which are issued by Cipci, or matters referred by him to the civilian police, which is page 27 of your report, paragraphs 3.53 to 3.54. And I'd like to just take you through a couple of these documents to ask you again why you have considered them to be of importance in relation to understanding this particular aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first document is D488, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And as it's coming onto the screen, it's a document dated the 7th of August, from Ivo Cipci to the 10th Police Station Sinj. Subject: Going of the Splitska Bank employees to Vrlika, Drnis, Knin, on the 8th of August, 1995. And there is reference in the text to: "We agree with the issuing of the passes and the request should be granted."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is that a document you recall having cited in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And can you assist us with why it was you considered that to be relevant, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, this is an example of instructions or decisions in relation to free movement, in which the police chief is issuing an instruction to a more junior member of the civil policing hierarchy without reference to the garrison commander in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document is D1111. It's a six-page document, but I'm just going to take you through a few of the pages as they deal with the same subject matter. It's a document you have referenced in your report, in support of your conclusions. And it's a document, the first page of which is the 9th of August, 1995, from Ivo Cipci again, to the 10th Police Station. And it refers to the passage of journalists and the approval of Assistant Minister of Defence, Mr. Markica Rebic, and Mr. -- Major-General Ivan Tolj. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And before I ask you to give us your observations on it, please, I would like you to see the second page, which is clearly linked to this page. And it's a document from Chief Djurica Franjo to the Zadar-Knin, Sibenik, Split-Dalmatia police administrations in respect of the same journalists. Now looking at those two documents together, please assist us with the importance, from your perspective, to this subject.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: The first page that was shown to me is an instruction coming out from the chief to the police station, in relation to the free movement of the journalists. The second page, in most police files, would be found behind the first page and would be the provenance or the explanation as to where the order came from and what the purpose was. So chronologically, I suppose you would look at the second page first, and you see there that under the provisions of the arrangement which was described in the 3rd of August document, which we discussed earlier, approval has been given by Messrs. Tolj and Rebic for these journalists to visit. That information has been transmitted by Mr. Djurica Franjo to Chief Cipci, who passes it on to the relevant police station. It's the operation of the Ministry of the Interior hierarchy, or chain of command, and the garrison commander whose TAOR might be affected by this is not informed or consulted in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One more example.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D1112, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's a similar form into the a document that you have seen and it's one that you cite. It's dated the 7th of August, 1995. It's, again, first page, from Ivo Cipci to the 10th Police Station, concerning a request for a visit to the region as set out in the subject matter. Does that look familiar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if I could now ask you to look at the second page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And why this document is of relevance to this section, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: It's a similar document which involves authority, in this case, for some political party officials to visit the area. And, again, the chain of command through which the authority is passed is the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you. I'd like to take you now to paragraph 3.55, please, on page 28 of the report. And, again, this paragraph here is one that you cite in support of your conclusion about events that took place concerning an EU monitoring team. The first document to look at, please, is D498, dated the 16th of August, from Ivo Cipci to the Ministry of the Interior, subject: Information on the presence of European monitors in the area of Vrlika. Referring to two European monitors at this stage not named, it appears from the document. On the front page. Do you have that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And then I'd like to you look at the second page of the document, please, towards the -- well, peruse the entire page. Mr. Albiston, before I ask you questions, I'd like to show you a second follow-up document so that we have the context of your observations --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Which is D497, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And I'd like you to see, this is a document, again, from Ivo Cipci, and he refers to "an attachment for your inspection," dated the 16th of August. So it's the same day. And if we go to the -- so that you have seen it, the second page of that document, here you see reference to submission of an attachment in the text. Well, we did do briefly. And we've gone now to the second page of that document which is, in fact, the report on the presence of these monitors in the area of Vrlika. Again, a document you cite. On the third page, which we have no need to go to, the names are provided of those monitors, and I'd like to you look at the fourth page, please, and the text under the heading number 2.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3.55 of your report, there's reference to both of these documents. And I'd like you to just expand upon, if you can, the reasons why you've brought these documents to our attention, in respect of the chapter heading for this section.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think, reading all the documents together, you can see that there seems to have been some confusion about who has what authority when, and what these documents show, and in particular the last two documents in relation to the two people who were stopped, is that General Cermak appears to have been attempting to provide some sort of informal authority for people to go to places in order to discharge their functions, when, in fact the Ministry of the Interior take a different view of how the procedure should have been operating and what the actual rules and regulations were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to follow on from that, I'd like you to see a document, please, which is not referred to in your report. It's P957. And I'd like to ask you, first of all, whether it's a document you recall in the review that you've conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, it's a document dated the 17th of August, author Marker Hansen, Hendriks, and it's to RC Knin from Team N2, an ECMM report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just take a look, Mr. Albiston, and see if that's a document you might have seen before? Because it's not in your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I have seen a significant number of documents which are ECMM documents. I can say that the material in the first paragraph which I have just read looks familiar, but I cannot tell this Chamber, as a matter of fact, that have I read this particular document in the creation of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to you read, please, paragraph 2 of that document that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gained the impression that when the witness was referring to paragraph 1, which consists of one word only, the word "calm," that he actually was referring already to paragraph 2, which he must have then read already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President is absolutely correct. I had read about the first seven or eight lines of what is paragraph 2 at the time that I made the remark, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please finish reading that. And since it is not entirely on your screen, I did not expect you to have it read in its entirety. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now my --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I've read as far as "political situation," which I --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: -- think may be what is required.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm interested in whether or not this document assists you either for or against the conclusions that you have made in respect of this particular incident and the role, or not, of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think it is entirely consistent with other documents in this case which I have seen, and I think it's particularly remarkable, if we look at the sixth line of paragraph 2, where it says in reference to General Cermak: "The General reacted immediately by phoning the minister of internal affairs and asking him to contact with the civil police in Split to establish coordination to avoid those accidents in future." I think what that indicates to us is that at the time of this incident, General Cermak is recognising the role of the -- what he describes or what the author of this document, I beg your pardon, describes as the minister of internal affairs, in other words the MUP hierarchy, as the authority which should have been dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to conclude on this series, can I have D499, please, which is dated 17th August, so the day after, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it's a document written by Josko -- signed by Josko Moric to the police administrations cited. And it's page 2 of that document that I would like to you look at and refresh your memory in respect of, as it's a document cited in your report. And, again, in the sequence of what we've been looking at, could you provide this Chamber with your observations as to the relevance of this document regarding the role of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- in my opinion, it demonstrates that the assistant minister for the interior, Mr. Moric, is the man who is making and communicating decisions about the requirements for passes, freedom of movement, and those sorts of issues within this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd now like to take you to different section of your report at this stage, which begins on the same page, page 28, and it deals with the subject of the investigation of crimes and other irregular acts. Do you have that section before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In this section you examined the allegation that Mr. Cermak failed to order either the military police or the civilian police to conduct investigations into crimes that had taken place. And if we turn to paragraph 3.56, which is on pages 28 over to 29, you conclude in your report that General Cermak had no statutory authority to initiate, conduct, direct, or supervise any criminal investigation. And for your purposes, that is supported by footnotes 110, 111, and 112. I'd like to understand how it was that you came to that conclusion, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the conclusion is based on an examination of the prevailing laws and procedures in the Republic of Croatia at this time, and the role which those laws and procedures accorded to various state officials. To some extent, there are parallels in relation to the military police, but I'm not here to discuss the way that the military police operated. But in relation to the civilian police and the role of the prosecutor and the role of the investigating judge, the documents which I have cited set out quite clearly what the functions of those individuals and those institutions is. And in common with most countries, the Republic of Croatia, in 1995, had a clear definition of the functions. It required trained state officials to carry out different functions, so that the civilian police would be responsible for securing scenes of crime, for initial investigations at the scene, and, in the case of serious crime, for assisting with subsequent investigations. And the role of the prosecutor, the role of the investigating judge, is set out, and I'm sure that there are many in this Chamber who have far better knowledge than I do of the details of that. But what is quite clear from those regulations is that nowhere is any role accorded to any military officer, any garrison commander, or any general, such as General Cermak. So that is why I conclude that, in fact, General Cermak did not have any responsibility, any rights, any locus in this area, and that, therefore, the suggestion in the indictment is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, from paragraph 3.60 onwards in that section, you review the actions that were taken by Mr. Moric, in terms of requesting reports on crimes and investigations from the civilian police, and requesting cooperation between the civilian and the military police. From a review of the documents that you undertook in that section, can you draw any conclusions about the actions taken by Mr. Moric within the Ministry of the Interior as regards the detection, processing and prevention of criminality after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The laws and regulations place the responsibility for civilian policing matters clearly at the feet of the assistant minister. And the sorts of matters which police -- civilian police are expected to deal with are similar to those in many countries: protection of life and property; the prevention of crime; assisting with the investigation of offences; the apprehension of offenders, and this sort of thing. And I think what this series of documents demonstrates is that Assistant Minister Mr. Moric was accepting his responsibilities and he was attempting to discharge those responsibilities through the medium of orders to and reports from the civilian police. And these documents are significant in numbers. They're clear in details, they are consistent, and they don't involve the garrison commander, General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Following on from that, if we turn to page 34 of your report and paragraph 3.71, you conclude that there is significant evidence that General Cermak was discharging his responsibilities, both as a citizen and as a senior representative of a state body, that he was passing and receiving information about crimes as part of a liaison role. And what I'd like to us do is examine -- we've already seen some of the documents you refer to there in your footnotes, but I would like to us look at the documents we have not yet seen on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first of which, please, D230.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Because I would like to us explain why it is you rely on these documents in respect of what you refer to as General Cermak discharging his responsibility as a citizen. Do you have that section of the report in front of you --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Albiston? The first document, D230, is a document --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 6th of September, 1995. And you see the subject, Sava Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we turn over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And see the author. It's from Chief Cedo Romanic. And information there provided in the first paragraph. Now, in respect of paragraph 3.71, why is this document of relevance, Mr. Albiston, to your conclusions? What is it you seek to rely on here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, this is a -- this is information coming from the police chief in relation to a serious crime and it's being supplied in direct response, as it says in the last paragraph, to an inquiry from the United Nations. And in my opinion, this demonstrates General Cermak's continuing liaison role.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. And you rely on it for that purpose in this regard for this paragraph, 3.71?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, it shows -- it shows a number of things but one of the things it shows is General Cermak participating, if you like, in the communication of information regarding crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now another document that we've already looked at, but I'll read it into the record for these purposes, is D487, under seal. I don't propose to bring it up on to the screen again but what I would do is ask for the next document, which is D500, and again it's in the same theme. You rely on it to support the same conclusion. It's a document from commander of the police station, Milos Mihic, dated the 13th of August, and it is partially legible. There are parts of it which are not legible as marked on the document, and it's reference there to gathered information from the members of the HV. And you can read the rest of the text yourself as it comes up onto the screen. Is that a familiar document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, why is this document significant as regards the content of this from Mr. Mihic in respect of this section, where you deal with General Cermak's responsibility as a citizen and the passing on or receiving of information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think this document has to be read in context with another document, and taken together, the documents demonstrate that General Cermak has passed on information concerning the taking of this vehicle, and that Mr. Mihic, the police commander, is asking the other police stations to assist in recovering this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What we're going to do is look at a series, a run of documents after the break in relation to these matters so I don't propose to call it up now, but it will be a document that comes back to us in our consideration of a further part of your report. Another example you cite in this section is D502, which is another document from Milos Mihic, dated the 13th of August, and it receives to -- to them having received a criminal complaint from the Ministry of Defence, Main Staff of HV Knin garrison, and it's addressed to the police administrations. Again, if you could cast your eye over the document and explain to the Chamber why it is of importance to this section.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. I think this -- this document shows us a couple of things, in relation to this particular issue that we're dealing with at the moment. That is to say, General Cermak complying with his obligation as a state official to ensure that crime is brought to the notice of the proper authorities. This document, taken with others, shows that, once again, Police Commander Mihic is seeking the assistance of other police stations to recover stolen property. And in the first paragraph he quite clearly states that it's the minister -- Ministry of Defence Main Staff of the Croatian Army, Knin garrison, which I think we can take as a reference to General Cermak. So, in this case, General Cermak is participating in the procedure for ensuring that crimes are brought to the attention of the relevant authorities in accordance with the legislation which I cited and which was mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, you cited legislation. Do you -- can you recall the provisions that you're referring to when you refer to General -- the obligation of a citizen or a state official in respect of passing on crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: It would be around about -- between 139 and 141, I think, the Article number of the relevant legislation. I would need to refer to the document to specify but it's certainly in that area of the Articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Albiston, and it's not in dispute that that is within the criminal procedural law, which is D1568. It's just for the purposes of clarity for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may deal with one more document quickly in this section before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if could you do that quickly because we're already at a time where we usually have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. The document is D505, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to round off this section, Mr. Albiston. It's another document you cite in your report. It's a document from Ivan Cermak to the police administration, Knin, dated the 19th of August, starting: "Dear gentlemen, we are attaching a memo from the president of the executive committee of the association of small shareholders." And again, why it is that you rely on this document and its relevance to the role of Mr. Cermak in respect of the section you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think there are a number of issues in this document, which to me, as a snap-shot, is a very, very significant document. It's significant partly for its content and partly for its style. If I address the issue of content first, in effect what is happening here is that the commander of the Knin garrison, General Cermak, is passing to the police information regarding a -- a police matter. And importantly, it says in the second paragraph: "... since we are not authorised for such and similar problems, we are therefore forwarding this memo to you." Now, I read that as a clear indication from the General that police matters are not matters for him. This is a civilian police matter. It is entirely distinct from his responsibilities. So that's the content. In relation to the style, "Dear gentlemen," and "respectfully," well, some senior police officers that I have dealt with have been quite polite, but have I never known them to address their subordinates in those sorts of terms. So this document is also significant to me, in indicating that General Cermak was not part of the hierarchy which he is addressing from the outside, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. Could I ask you, as far as time is concerned, whether we are on track.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm relatively confident that we are. It would just be -- if I don't conclude this session, it would be a matter of 15 minutes in the next session tomorrow. But I'm getting through as I had hoped to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because your estimate was three sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now if we would follow all the estimates, even if we would take four to six sessions to be five, then we would not conclude this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify, our estimate has actually changed to up to eight sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that in view of the remaining time this week and the time next week, that we really might get in trouble to finish your last witness - that's not you, Mr. Albiston - by next week Wednesday. Even if we would have some additional time available. Could I ask the parties to really thoroughly consider, in view of what apparently is sought to be achieved, to see where time can be gained without losing content. We'll have a -- yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We were talking at the break, my colleague and I, Mr. Misetic, and, of course, we'll talk to the client, and tried to hone down our estimate of two sessions. I don't think, in light of some of the presentation that we have had this morning, that we are going to need quite that time. Frankly, I don't think we'll even -- if we move into some of the areas, depends what happens in the next session, if we move into some of these areas, it should be significantly less than one session. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you said moved down to two sessions but the estimate which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was one to two sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. And my moving down is less than one session, and again I just want to consult with my client and Mr. Misetic concerning a few issues. But I thought I would bring that to the attention of the Chamber at this juncture, as it is considering time estimates for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Mr. Albiston, you will be aware that the parties are discussing how to use their time, but they certainly are aware that it's your time as well. We will have a break and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, we are now moving to the section of your report entitled: The garrison commander and the prevention of crime, which is at page 34. In that section you start off by addressing the Prosecution pre-trial brief paragraph 81. The allegation of which is that Mr. Cermak should have taken necessary and reasonable measures to prevent his subordinates from committing crimes. You make your observations and conclusions at several points in your report that the civilian police were not subordinated to Mr. Cermak. What I'd like to go on to look at it is a conclusion that you make that the responsibility for the prevention of crime lay with the Ministry of the Interior. Now, in support of that conclusion you refer to numerous documents, which include D1077, D41, D583, and D411. I'd like to us look at two documents from this selection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If could I ask that D50 be brought onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And this is a document from that particular section. We're going to look at the document and the next document, in turn, and I'm going to ask you why it is they support your conclusion and what observations you have to assist this Trial Chamber with the determinations that it has to make? The first document, D50, is dated the 22nd of August, 1995, and we see it is addressed to various police administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We know that from the following page it is sent by Josko Moric. And can you see here, on page 2: "Measures that are set out in order for us to monitor the problem at the state level." And you can see the provisions that are made there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if we could just go to the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It refers to a telegram and a reference to: "In order to stop houses being burnt and other people's movable property being taken away unlawfully in the liberated territory." Before I ask you a question on that document, I'd like to move to the second one. Similar theme --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Which is D574, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, it's a document from Josko Moric. This one is dated the 30th of August, 1995. And on the first page of that document, we will see a reference to the request of: "... a report on linkage with the military police in order to prevent further torching of houses and illegal taking of movable property from rightful owners in liberated territories." Now I have chosen two examples. You may be asked about others in due course, but could you assist with us these two particular examples, Mr. Albiston, as to why you have included them here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is the operation, once again, of the Ministry of the Interior hierarchy. The acceptance of the responsibilities which I've suggested are conventional to a Ministry of the Interior, which runs a civilian police organisation, and instructions from the assistant minister to the heads of the police administrations to deal with the issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you also refer, among other documents, these are documents that we've mentioned before, the Law of the Interior, D1077; the criminal law of Croatia, which you've looked at, 65 ter 1780.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The Decree on Internal Organisation of the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D527. In your review of those documents, legislation, did you find any provision which would support the allegation that General Cermak had a duty to prevent crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next section to touch upon, if we may, is entitled: The garrison commander and the punishment of criminal behaviour. And that begins at page 39 to 40 of your report; Croatian, page 38 to 39. In paragraph 3.84 of that report, you say that General Cermak had no legal duty to punish criminal behaviour of civilian police after Operation Storm. And I refer you to both paragraph 3.83 through to 3.85. Can you expand upon the reasons behind your opinion and conclusion in this regard, Mr. Albiston, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to General Cermak's authority, I will restrict my remarks, as always, to his authority, in relation to the civilian police, and it seems to me, from looking at the documents and from my knowledge of the issues which face this Chamber, that there are two matters to consider. The one is whether General Cermak was in a position to punish crimes, as it's suggested. That is to say, to deal with serious crimes through the criminal justice system. And the other issue is whether General Cermak was in a position to exercise any form of disciplinary authority over the civilian police. Now, in relation to the first matter, which I think is really the issue before this Chamber, and I'll explain why I say that in a minute. I think I've probably already addressed this Chamber on the legal and constitutional position and where the responsibility lay under law for both the prevention of crime and the investigation and punishment of criminal offences, and that that is set out and that there are roles within the criminal justice system for the civilian police and the prosecutor and the investigating judge, but there is no role for the garrison commander, or other military figures in relation to the civilian police and any criminal offences which civilian police officers might have committed. In relation to the discipline matters, I think there are two points to make. The first is in relation to what I said earlier, about why I make the distinction about what the Chamber is interested in. In my reading of these documents, I do not think that we're talking about disciplinary offences, which would normally be handled within a police disciplinary regime. The sort of matters which have been brought before this Chamber are grave crimes. But there is a disciplinary mechanism within the civilian police of the Republic of Croatia, and in 1995, that is set out and there is a document which I think the number is 588, probably P588, but it is a sort of a brochure which is in Croatian and in English and is illustrated and sets out in fairly simple terms the structures of the Ministry of the Interior. And I'm sure that the Chamber has this document which can be called up. The reason I mention it, is that it alludes, as any police officer would expect it to, to the internal discipline procedures of the Croatian police. So these internal disciplinary procedures exist, but there is no role within these procedures, again, as any police expert would expect, for a garrison commander. It simply isn't there. On that basis, in my opinion, General Cermak did not have any role in the matters to which this part of the indictment relates.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Following on to the next subject you deal with which is examples of General Cermak's lack of authority. And I'm going to take you to three different areas, three different subjects that you rely upon under the heading of the garrison commander UNCRO and examples of General Cermak's lack of authority. That can be found at page 40 to 43 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D303, please, to be brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to start firstly, Mr. Albiston, with the issue of the attempts that were made to retrieve UN vehicles and equipment. And it's something that you have already referred to in the evidence that you have given today to this Court. The first document in the series we're going to look at, as it comes up onto the screen, D303, it's entitled: Order. It's -- the name Ivan Cermak there appears at the bottom and it's dated the 9th of August, 1995. And it refers to the following in paragraph 1: "Immediately set up a team." Do you see that document before you there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now is there anything that you can say, Mr. Albiston, to assist this Chamber, based on your professional experience, about the way in which this order is written, first of all, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, to me, the style doesn't look like an order as part of a police hierarchical system, and there's a particular reason for that, which is that it's addressed, if we look at the bottom left-hand corner -- well, it's certainly bottom left-hand corner in the English translation. It's addressed to the commander of the Knin military police, the commander of the Knin police station, and files here. Now in my experience, in a hierarchical situation it is very difficult to address an order to two different individuals without specifying how you expect that order to be complied with. Similarly, the instruction is to set up a team with the task the finding vehicles. That's -- I think the meaning is -- is clear, but I don't think that the style in which it is conveyed is consistent with what I would expect to find in police orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, let look at the next document in the series, which is D503, which is several days later, on the 12th of August, and is a further document entitled: Order. From Ivan Cermak. And, again, it relates to the forming of teams consisting of members of the MUP from the Knin police station and from the Knin military police with the task of finding and returning the stolen UNCRO equipment and vehicles. If you could look at the first page of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And then I would ask that you see the second page so you can see the entirety of the document and the order that was given. Now, once again, what can you tell us, based on your professional experience, about the -- firstly, the way in which this order is written, if anything?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, I think the language is more directive. In particular, if we look at the last two paragraphs, it suggests that the author of the document is quite keen that the recipients of the document should respond to it -- deal with it and respond to it. But I'm afraid as an order, it still suffers from the same difficulty of being addressed to more than one person. And if I were in receipt of that, I would be seeking clarification as to whether I or the other named recipient was actually the person that was going have to answer to the author on the outcome of the matter. My view is that these two documents -- actually it is difficult to sustain the argument that they are orders because they're not going people in the hierarchy who can receive orders, and there are other documents which might need to be considered to set this in context.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, let's look at those. The next one is D304, which may assist you. And it's a letter from Ivan Cermak to the Military District Command, attention, Chief of Staff, subject: Report on the behaviour of a part of members of the HV. It consists of only two paragraphs. So if could you just remind yourself again of the content, which perhaps may assist you in answering the questions on this area of the UNCRO vehicles and equipment.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen the first page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, why have you relied upon this in your section on UNCRO and examples of General Cermak's lack of authority, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me, from the text of the document, that it is tantamount to admission by General Cermak that actually he is not getting anywhere with the steps which he has taken, and that he realises that if he wants action from the military in relation to recovery of the vehicles, then it's to the military command that he needs to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Document D305, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 13th of August, from Ante Gotovina, Colonel General, in the form of an order, dated, as I said, the 13th, and it refers to the return of the vehicles stolen. You have cited this document in this section of the report. Again, if you just remind yourself.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We see on page 2 who this document was forwarded to for action.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, your reason for inclusion into this section, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Well, it's part of the same story, so to speak, it's a continuation of this matter of the stolen vehicles. And, of course, this document, like the other two which I was discussing, or the two previous to the last one, is addressed to more than one recipient. But it doesn't suffer from the same ambiguities that having multiple addressees might create, because what this document is saying is, We don't want this sort of thing happening, and, by the way, if any of you addressees have got these vehicles, let's have them back. So I think the difficulty which I identified with the previous documents as orders doesn't apply to this one. This is much clearer. And whether it is consistent with other military documents, of course, would be for a military expert to say. But I think this one fits in with the story of the missing vehicles very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In D500, please, next, a document that we have already looked at which triggered your reference, in fact, earlier to there being a chain of documents in this regard. It's a document that you will recall, I'm sure, having looked at it just an hour ago. And, again, what I'm interested in its relevance in terms of the authority or not of the original orders which you saw from Mr. Cermak, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just for the record, it's dated 13th of August. It's a document from Milos Mihic, and it refers to the gathering of information in respect of a Toyota Land Cruiser and other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the way that I read this document is that Mr. Mihic, the commander of the Knin police station, is ensuring that information he's received from General Cermak regarding the stolen vehicles is available to the other police stations so that should these vehicles be found, they can be returned accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Does it tell you anything about Milos Mihic's attitude towards the original order or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: He uses the expression "gathered information." He doesn't suggest that he is acting on the instructions of a garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the final document, please, D502.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, we looked at this before. Document from Milos Mihic, 13th of August, referring to different equipment and vehicles. I'm interested in its relevance to the issue of authority of Mr. Cermak and also how Milos Mihic interprets the information, as best you can say, if at all, that he received in respect of the order.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. The wording is very similar, particularly in the last paragraph. The detailed information in the middle section is different, of course, and in the first section I think it is a little bit clearer that Mr. Mihic is regarding General Cermak as the vehicle for conveying information about a -- a crime from the complainant and into the civilian policing system.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What, if any, assistance did you glean in the writing of your report from having reviewed the testimony of Witness 86 in this trial, as we know you have because you referred to it, and I'm interested particularly in respect of the Cermak orders that we have looked at in this regard?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I think there are -- there's more than one instance in that particular witness's oral testimony to this Chamber to suggest that, in relation to these matters, that witness believed that the orders, as they appear on paper, from General Cermak, were treated by the civilian police as being pieces of information regarding a crime that had been committed, and that indeed there are examples within the oral testimony of that particular witness, which suggests that he did not believe that General Cermak had any authority to issue orders to the civilian police on this or any other matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D487, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We have looked at this document before. It is the second example, if you like, that you cite to support your conclusion that Mr. Cermak did not have authority. And I'm asking you now from that particular perspective of a lack of authority and what it is in that document that you seek to rely on, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we saw this document earlier today, and I particularly draw the attention of the Chamber to the first paragraph and the last paragraph. The verbal request for a statement is not, in my experience, indicative of authority; authority by General Cermak over the author of this document. The request, it's repeated, comes as a result of an inquiry from the international community, which it reinforces the idea that in this particular case the reason for the existence of the communication which is communicating about a crime, is that General Cermak has been approached in his capacity as the interlocutor or representative of the Croatian authorities by a member of the international community. And again I would draw the Chamber's attention to the third paragraph or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- final paragraph might be more accurate to say, and refer to the remarks which I made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Higgins, would a reference to the remarks and observations made earlier, would that not have done --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how I intend to deal with the next example, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next example and final example that you rely on we have already looked, and it's D505. I don't intend to recall it back on the screen. It's the letter that you spoke to -- told us about, from Ivan Cermak headed: "Dear gentlemen ..."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And we already have your observations in that regard on this matter.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The penultimate issue I wish to deal with you with is in terms of the Croatian police and UNCIVPOL, and this is pages 43 to 46 of your report in the Croatian, and 44 onwards in the English version. Now, you have reviewed, during the course of your engagement in this case, the relationship between UNCIVPOL and the Croatian civilian police, and I'm interested in whether or not that relationship reveals anything to you, as a professional police officer, about the position or role of Mr. Cermak as regards the civilian police, particularly given the allegations in this case that Mr. Cermak was superior to the civilian police. Could you assist the Chamber with that, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: Yes. I have looked at a significant number of documents which relate to UNCIVPOL matters and their relationship with the Croatian civilian police. In particular, I was concerned to look at this because of General Cermak's role as an interlocutor with the international community. But what comes through, clearly, taking the documents as a whole, is that police officers dealt with police officers, and, on the basis of my professional experience, I am not at all surprised to find that. The police officers were dealing with police issues. The responsibilities of the UNCIVPOL mission related primarily to monitoring duties, and the people that they would be concerned to be in touch with would be their opposite numbers within the Croatian civilian police, and I think that that's what the documents show.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to follow on from that point, in paragraph 3.99 of your report, you refer to the fact that records show that UNCIVPOL frequently reported crimes to the Croatian police. Do you have any observations on this reporting of crime line by international police officers to local police and its significance, if any?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I think it's not surprising that it should take place, particularly if UNCIVPOL officers were moving in areas where the Croatian civilian police were not operating or not operating at the same time. That, in those circumstances, the UNCIVPOL officers may well, on occasions, have been the first officers to discover scenes of crime, or to have crime reported to them by members of the public, and that they participated in the system by passing on information regarding those crimes to their Croatian civilian police counterparts. And we know from other documents that there were delays and difficulties in establishing an effective civilian police presence by the Croatian police throughout the area concerned, and in other areas, I discuss geography and numbers and so on. So there would, of course, be occasions when the first police officers at a scene or the first police officers available for approach by the public would in fact be a United Nations rather than Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That brings me on to the final question that I have for you, Mr. Albiston, which relates to the issue of civilian police manpower. What conclusions are you able to draw and expand upon in respect of the resources that you have seen available to the police in the months following Operation Storm, the varying commitment of the military police to assist, the lack of vehicles, equipment, et cetera, which you referred to in your report, and how that may have impacted upon the work of the police in the territory.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON
utterances.text: I -- the temptation in answer to that question is to take up an awful a lot of the Chamber's time, so I will try to be mindful of that problem. There are, in policing circles, ways of approaching the question of manpower establishment. As I indicate in the report, there are different figures in different jurisdictions which are regarded as being the norm, and a figure of one police officer per 400 head of population would not be particularly surprising. But I hesitated in the report, as I would hesitate in live evidence to this Chamber, to specify the number of police or civilian police that I think would be appropriate for policing in this area at this time. And there are a number of reasons for that. The population was in a flux in terms of its size and its movements. There was a large irregular presence of troops. There -- the situation was immediate post-conflict, which creates additional problems for police; for example, in terms of moving about, because of the possibility of mines, unexploded ordnance, poor road maps, destroyed roads, and so on. Many of the police that were drafted in would have been unfamiliar with the area, so there are all sorts of reasons why policing would be difficult, and one of the ways of addressing difficulties for policing would be to have greater numbers of police. What I think we can say, rather than try to specify the size of the population and the numbers of reported crimes and the distances that needed to be travelled, and from that to derive some sort of formula which is consistent with other parts of the Republic of Croatia in terms of allocation of police manpower, I think it's probably more helpful to look at the incidents which took place and the comments on those incidents by both the civilian police officers and the police coordinators that the Chamber has heard were appointed to assist with re-establishing normal civilian policing at this time. And they point to a number of difficulties in relation to police manpower issues. For example, as is quite common in immediate post-conflict situation, a lot of police manpower was deployed to guarding vulnerable sites, and vulnerable sites could take the form of economic or military institutions. They could take the form of sensitive locations such as what we used call patrimonial sites, for example, protecting churches which would be the churches of minority in an area where there had been conflict. Patrolling, check-points, all these sorts of duties are sapping on police manpower. And I draw attention in my report to an example of a police commander discussing his manpower issues, and my comment is that it seems a very modest demand, in view of my own professional assessment of the sort of requirements that he would have, in order to discharge the duties which were placed upon him by the civilian police hierarchy. So, to be as brief as possible, I would say that there were significant difficulties for civilian policing, that those difficulties meant that manpower was a particularly important issue, that the evidence of the documents suggests that manpower was not adequate to meet all the requirements. For example, whilst the civilian police are seen in a number of documents to complain that the military police do not support them in check-points, the UNCIVPOL police officers are similarly reporting occasions on which the Croatian civilian police failed to meet them and turn up to perform check-points, and sometimes the explanation for this is lack of manpower and sometimes it's lack of vehicles. So there were all sorts of problems that would impact upon police and make it difficult to establish satisfactory manpower levels. I accept that very few senior police officers ever say, I've got enough people. It doesn't work like that. But I think there are legitimate reasons for believing the police coordinators and the police commanders who felt under pressure in terms of the responsibilities which were placed on them by comparison with the resources which were allocated to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, thank you for that lengthy answer. I have no further questions for you.
